title: Systems Programming: C, Processes & Concurrency
subtitle: Reason about bytes, ownership and coordination from a C program to a parallel system.
description: Learn C and systems programming in manageable steps. Start with small programs, draw memory and resource ownership, then build complete tools with files, processes and threads.
coverage: A complete C11 and POSIX path with 24 chapters and 57 standalone programs. A six-pass study plan leads to three fully worked engineering projects. Follow requirements, interfaces, complete source, debugging and tests. Deeper branches remain available as reference.
prerequisites: Basic programming with variables, loops and functions
Comfort reading short C expressions and terminal commands
outcomes: Trace C objects, pointers and lifetimes without relying on undefined behavior
Explain compilation, linkage and resource ownership
Choose and reason about Unix process and IPC mechanisms
Coordinate threads using explicit invariants and synchronization
Evaluate parallel performance with appropriate measurements

map.purpose: Understand how values are stored and when pointers may access objects, then organize text, structures and dynamic data.

map.purpose: Follow source into running processes through preprocessing, linking, signals and child-process lifecycles.

map.purpose: Partition correct computations into parallel work, then check performance and correctness using equivalent workloads and reproducible evidence.

topics.title: Bits, C types and explicit control
topics.story:
A shipping label can contain the same printed digits while meaning a quantity, a product code or a price. Computer bits similarly acquire meaning through a representation and a type. A byte is storage, not an instruction to interpret it as a letter or a signed number. C asks the programmer to be explicit about these choices, then uses control flow to decide which operations run.

A function receives copies of its arguments, much like a clerk receiving a copied form; changing the copy does not change the original form unless the form contains a usable reference to it.
topics.principle:
A positional numeral sums digit values multiplied by powers of its base. C integer types have finite ranges; unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo one more than the maximum representable value, while overflowing signed arithmetic is undefined behavior. Integer division truncates toward zero in modern C; use a floating operand when a fractional result is intended. sizeof yields an object size in C bytes and has type size_t; a byte contains CHAR_BIT bits, not a universally fixed eight.

Initialize automatic objects before reading them. Conditions treat zero as false and nonzero as true; && and || short-circuit, unlike bitwise operators. Loops need clear bounds and progress. Functions have declared parameter and result types, pass arguments by value and should express whether a result or error is being returned.
topics.formula:
Value of digits aₘ…a₀ in base B = Σᵢ aᵢBⁱ
Unsigned range with w value bits: 0 … 2ʷ−1
Unsigned result = mathematical result mod 2ʷ
Loop invariant example: sum = Σⱼ₌₀ⁱ⁻¹ a[j]
topics.symbols:
B is a numeral base, aᵢ a digit between zero and B−1, and i its position counting from the right. The unsigned formula uses w value bits, excluding any padding bits. It does not describe signed overflow. In the loop invariant, i is the number of already processed array elements and sum their accumulated value, assuming the additions remain representable.

An invariant describes what stays true at each loop boundary and helps justify both correctness and bounds.
topics.example:
The binary numeral 101101 equals 32+8+4+1=45, which is hexadecimal 2D. On a machine with an eight-bit unsigned char, converting the mathematical value 260 to that type produces 4. In contrast, adding one to the maximum signed int has no portable numeric answer. For a three-element array {2,4,7}, start sum=0 and i=0.

Each loop adds a[i] and increments i; successive sums are 2, 6 and 13. The condition i<3 prevents an invalid fourth access. The expression 13/3 produces integer 4, while 13.0/3 produces an approximate floating result of 4.3333.
topics.pitfall: Do not infer a language guarantee from one machine’s observed overflow result. Unsigned wrap is specified; signed overflow is not.

check.question: Why does a function taking int x fail to change the caller’s integer when it assigns x=9?
check.answer: The parameter is a separate object initialized from the argument value. Return the new value or pass a pointer to the caller’s object and modify that object through the pointer.

glossary.meaning: An integer value with no negative range; arithmetic uses a defined modulus.
A case for which the C standard imposes no behavior requirements.
A fact preserved at a chosen program boundary.

guided_questions.question: Can a successful run prove signed overflow is safe?
guided_questions.answer: No. Undefined behavior is not made valid by one observed result. Guard before arithmetic.

guided_questions.question: Why cast before division?
guided_questions.answer: Converting the completed integer quotient cannot recover the discarded fraction.

guided_questions.question: What does sizeof count?
guided_questions.answer: C bytes. CHAR_BIT states how many bits a byte has on the implementation.

instructor_notes.title: Separate representation from meaning
instructor_notes.body: A numeric identifier and a quantity may share an integer type but need different validation. The type range is only the outer boundary of the domain.

instructor_notes.title: Choose overflow behavior deliberately
instructor_notes.body: Unsigned wrap is useful for modular arithmetic, but a wrapped allocation size or item count is usually a defect. Defined behavior can still violate the intended contract.

code_examples.intro: Use implementation limits without executing signed overflow.
code_examples.output:

signed addition rejected
integer quotient=4
floating quotient=4.3333
code_examples.explanation:
UINT_MAX plus one wraps to zero for every conforming unsigned int representation. The signed branch checks the limit before addition, so no signed overflow is executed.

The final pair changes operand types before division. Four decimal places are an output format, not a claim that the binary floating representation is exact.

topics.title: Pointers, arrays and multidimensional layout
topics.story:
An apartment directory has a building address, a floor number and a room number. Knowing an address is useful only when the building exists and the requested room belongs to it. A C pointer similarly needs a valid object and a live storage duration before dereferencing. Pointer arithmetic moves by objects of the pointed-to type, like taking one floor at a time rather than one centimeter.

A two-dimensional array is a building with equally sized floors; an array of pointers is a collection of directions that may lead to unrelated buildings. Similar-looking notation can hide very different layouts.
topics.principle:
A pointer stores a pointer value, and dereferencing accesses the designated object when type, alignment, lifetime and bounds requirements hold. Arrays contain contiguous elements, but an array object is not a pointer variable. In most expressions an array converts to a pointer to its first element; sizeof and unary & are important exceptions.

Pointer arithmetic is defined within an array and one past its end; the one-past pointer may be formed but not dereferenced. Subtracting pointers requires the same array and yields ptrdiff_t. A real T[R][C] is an array of R row arrays, so its usual converted type is pointer to a C-element row. It is not T**. An array parameter is adjusted to a pointer parameter, so pass length explicitly.
topics.formula:
a[i] ≡ *(a+i), for valid i
Array bytes = N·sizeof(T)
Row-major byte offset of a[r][c] = (r·C+c)·sizeof(T)
int a[R][C] converts to int (*)[C], not int **
topics.symbols:
N is the number of elements of a one-dimensional array and T their type. In the row-major offset, r and c are zero-based row and column indices and C the number of columns; all indices must be in range. The offset describes object layout in bytes rather than permission to cross subarray bounds with an arbitrary scalar pointer.

A pointer-to-row advances by one complete row. Array-to-pointer conversion does not carry the array’s length into a function.
topics.example:
Assume sizeof(int)=4 and declare int grid[2][3]={{2,4,6},{8,10,12}}. The array occupies 2×3×4=24 bytes. Element grid[1][2] is at byte offset (1×3+2)×4=20 from the start. A pointer declared int (*row)[3]=grid advances 12 bytes when incremented once; row[1][2] accesses 12. By contrast, int *p=grid[0] points into the first three-element row. p+3 is its one-past pointer and must not be dereferenced as a portable way to access the next row.

Use the row-aware type and indices to express the actual array structure. This distinction matters even though the rows occupy adjacent storage bytes.
topics.pitfall: Inside a function parameter declared int a[], sizeof(a) measures a pointer. It cannot recover the caller’s array element count.

check.question: Can a pointer one past a five-element array be used in a loop comparison?
check.answer: Yes, it can serve as the end sentinel and be compared appropriately with pointers into the same array. Dereferencing that sentinel is invalid.

glossary.meaning: The live object designated by a pointer.
A valid array boundary marker that must not be dereferenced.
A pointer whose pointed-to type is a whole row array.

guided_questions.question: Does a pointer remember the array length?
guided_questions.answer: Not by itself. Pass a length alongside the pointer or encode a valid boundary separately.

guided_questions.question: Why is int ** not a two-dimensional array type?
guided_questions.answer: It points to an int pointer object. A real grid converts to a pointer to an array row, with different layout and stepping.

guided_questions.question: May an end pointer be read as an element?
guided_questions.answer: No. It may mark the boundary, but dereferencing one past the array is invalid.

instructor_notes.title: Keep bounds beside addresses
instructor_notes.body: An address alone is not a complete buffer contract. Carry count, capacity and ownership separately when each has a different meaning.

instructor_notes.title: Preserve row structure in types
instructor_notes.body: A pointer-to-row lets the compiler scale arithmetic correctly. Flatten only through a deliberately defined one-dimensional representation, not by ignoring subarray bounds.

code_examples.title: Start here: a copy and an address
code_examples.intro: Follow one integer before learning array pointer arithmetic. Predict every printed value first.
code_examples.output:
inside copy=9
after value call: original=4 copy=4
after address call: original=9 copy=4
code_examples.explanation:
Imagine two paper notes. Copying the number onto a second note does not link the notes. A pointer instead carries the location of the first note. Both function parameters are passed by value. The second function receives a copied address and uses it to change the original object.

&original means the address of original. *address means the integer at that valid address. In int *alias, the star is part of a declaration; in *address = 9, it is a dereference expression. The original object is still alive during both calls. This helper requires a valid non-null pointer to an int.
walkthrough: Create two independent int objects with the same initial value.
Pass a copied number; only the function parameter changes.
Pass a copied address; dereferencing reaches the caller’s original object.

syntax_notes.meaning: Store the address, not another integer value.
Write the object reached through this valid pointer.
Copy the argument value into the parameter.

code_examples.title: Traverse with a begin and end pointer
code_examples.intro: Use the end as a sentinel, never as an element.
code_examples.explanation:
Array conversion supplies a pointer to the first element. Adding count forms one past the end. The comparison happens before dereferencing, so the sentinel is never read.

Both pointers in the subtraction belong to the same array. Their difference counts elements, not bytes, and %td matches ptrdiff_t. The sum is safe for these fixed inputs.
walkthrough: Create begin and one-past end from the same array.
Dereference only while the cursor differs from end.
Subtract same-array pointers to recover the traversed count.

syntax_notes.meaning: Point to integers read through this pointer without modifying them. const does not extend lifetime.
Form the one-past boundary inside the permitted array arithmetic range.
Access the element designated by a valid in-range pointer.

code_examples.title: Use the actual row type
code_examples.intro: Traverse a rectangular array through a pointer to a three-element row.
code_examples.output:
row 0 sum=12
row 1 sum=30
second row last=12
row elements=3
code_examples.explanation:
Parentheses bind *row before [3], so row points to an array of three ints. Adding one advances by one complete row, and the second index stays within that row.

The final sizeof ratio counts row elements without assuming sizeof(int). No pointer into the first scalar row is used to cross its one-past boundary.
walkthrough: Declare the pointer with its row width.
Use separate row and column bounds.
Check row stepping and row length independently.

topics.title: Strings, bounded input and parsing
topics.story:
A train of character cars needs a clearly marked final car so a worker knows when to stop reading. In a C string, the zero byte supplies that marker; the buffer’s physical capacity is a separate fact. A worker who keeps walking until a marker appears can leave the allocated track if no marker exists. Input complicates the job because the arriving train may be longer than the track.

Safe text handling records capacity, checks how much arrived and decides what to do with leftover input. It also distinguishes the characters representing a number from the numeric value itself.
topics.principle:
A C string is a sequence of characters terminated by a null character. Its logical length excludes the terminator, while storage must include it. strlen requires a valid terminated string, and strcmp compares contents rather than pointer addresses. String literals must not be modified; a character array initialized from a literal can be modified within bounds. fgets limits the number stored and may retain a newline or return only part of a long line, so detect truncation where line integrity matters.

A scanf %s conversion needs a width and a checked return count. strtol supports validated numeric conversion through an end pointer and range reporting, unlike unchecked atoi. Functions from ctype.h require EOF or a value representable as unsigned char; cast potentially negative char values before classification.
topics.formula:
Required capacity ≥ strlen(text)+1
fgets(buffer,C,stream): at most C−1 characters plus terminator when C>1
Valid parsed integer = digits consumed ∧ permitted suffix ∧ no range error
topics.symbols:
C is the destination buffer capacity in bytes, and strlen counts bytes before the first null character, not necessarily user-perceived Unicode characters. The added one reserves the terminator. The parsing expression is a checklist, not a quantitative equation: verify that some digits were consumed, any remaining characters are allowed, and conversion did not exceed the target range.

A bounded read protects the destination size but does not itself prove that a complete logical line was consumed.
topics.example:
A buffer char name[6] can store at most five ordinary single-byte name characters plus the terminator. Reading the line Maple followed by newline with fgets(name,6,stdin) stores M,a,p,l,e,zero; the newline remains in the stream. The program must consume or otherwise account for the remaining line before the next logical read.

For numeric input "42x", strtol with base 10 produces 42 and points the end pointer at x. A strict integer parser rejects that suffix. Input " 42 " can be accepted if the policy permits surrounding whitespace and verifies the remaining characters are only whitespace.
topics.pitfall: Using strncpy does not automatically produce a terminated string when the input fills the bound. Choose a deliberate copying policy and verify capacity and termination.

check.question: Why is char *p="lamp" different from char a[]="lamp"?
check.answer: p points to a string literal that must not be modified. a is a separate modifiable five-element array containing the four letters and the null terminator.

glossary.meaning: The zero character marking the end of a C string.
The total number of bytes available in a destination buffer.
A pointer returned by conversion to the first unconsumed character.

guided_questions.question: Is strlen the buffer capacity?
guided_questions.answer: No. It counts bytes before the first terminator and requires that a valid terminator already exists.

guided_questions.question: Why reject 42x after strtol returns 42?
guided_questions.answer: The numeric prefix is valid but the suffix violates a strict whole-input integer contract.

guided_questions.question: Why cast char before isspace?
guided_questions.answer: A negative plain char other than EOF is outside the function’s permitted argument domain.

instructor_notes.title: A bounded operation can still lose a record
instructor_notes.body: Preventing a buffer overflow does not ensure a full logical line was received. Decide whether to reject, accumulate or intentionally truncate long records.

instructor_notes.title: Parsing is a policy boundary
instructor_notes.body: Decide whether signs and surrounding whitespace are accepted before choosing library calls. A successful conversion alone does not validate the whole domain.

code_examples.title: Start here: a string needs an ending byte
code_examples.intro: Look at a short character array before using a parser.
code_examples.output:
capacity=6 length=2
character 0=H
character 1=i
terminator is zero=yes
after edit=Ho
code_examples.explanation:
A six-seat row can hold two people and still have empty seats. Capacity is the storage available; string length counts characters before the first zero byte. The string literal initializes H, i, and the terminator. The remaining array elements are also zero-initialized.

strlen assumes that a terminator is reachable in valid storage. It does not check a buffer’s capacity for you. Changing message[1] changes i to o without moving the terminator. sizeof message works here because message is the array object in this scope. A function parameter written char message[] would be adjusted to a pointer.
walkthrough: Separate the capacity six from the payload length two.
Inspect only the two characters and their in-bounds terminator.
Edit one character while preserving the terminator.

syntax_notes.meaning: Reserve six bytes and initialize a terminated string.
Count bytes before the first zero, assuming valid terminated storage.
The zero character used to end a C string; it is not the printed digit zero.

code_examples.title: Return success separately from the result
code_examples.intro: Build a tiny parser with an explicit failure guarantee before reading strtol.
code_examples.output:
text='0' accepted=1 result=0
text='7' accepted=1 result=7
text='12' accepted=0 result=-1
text='' accepted=0 result=-1
text='x' accepted=0 result=-1
code_examples.explanation:
A valid result can itself be zero. Therefore zero cannot mean both “the parsed value is zero” and “parsing failed”. This interface returns a success flag and writes the number through a separate pointer only on success. Invalid text leaves the caller’s result unchanged.

The first guard also handles an empty string: its first byte is zero, outside the digit range, so the function returns before reading text[1]. If the first byte is a digit, a valid terminated input string has a following byte to inspect. C guarantees that decimal digit characters are consecutive, so subtracting the character zero gives the numeric digit. The contract accepts exactly one digit, not signs or spaces. Both pointers must be valid; text must be terminated.
walkthrough: Write the accepted language first: one digit and then a terminator.
Run all guards before touching the output object.
Check both the success flag and the preserved value on rejected input.

syntax_notes.meaning: A caller-owned output object, not a return status.
Reject without changing *result.
Convert one validated digit character into its integer value.

code_examples.title: Separate text length from storage capacity
code_examples.intro: Observe a terminated copy and explicitly detect a truncated formatted result.
code_examples.output:
text=Lamp length=4 capacity=5
stored=Map required=5
truncated=yes
code_examples.explanation:
The array text owns five bytes and permits changing its first letter. strlen reports four because it excludes the terminator.

With capacity four, snprintf stores three letters and a terminator. Its result five reports the full intended length, excluding the terminator. Comparing that result to capacity detects truncation instead of silently treating Map as the full name.
walkthrough: Inspect the array size and the terminated text length.
Write through a bounded formatting function.
Check the returned required length against capacity.

syntax_notes.meaning: Create a modifiable array containing four letters and a zero terminator.
Measure this actual array’s capacity in bytes, including the terminator.
Limit writes by capacity and return the length that would have been produced without the bound.

code_examples.title: Validate the entire integer input
code_examples.intro: Accept surrounding spaces while rejecting suffixes, empty text and range failures.
code_examples.output:
input 0 rejected
input 1 accepted=42
input 2 rejected
input 3 rejected
code_examples.explanation:
strtol reads a numeric prefix and exposes where it stopped. The helper rejects no digits, long overflow, and values outside int before casting. It then allows only trailing whitespace.

The output pointer is updated only after every check succeeds, so rejected inputs preserve the caller’s previous value. This helper assumes non-null pointers to a valid terminated string and writable int.
walkthrough: Reset errno and record the first unconsumed character.
Check both conversion range and destination type range.
Commit the output only when the entire text is accepted.

topics.title: Structures, alignment, unions and tags
topics.story:
A toolbox groups a ruler, a hammer and a screwdriver into one kit even though they are different shapes. A struct groups different C member types into one object. Protective spaces between tools resemble padding added for alignment: the box may be larger than the sum of its contents. A union is closer to a case with interchangeable inserts, where several representations share storage.

A tag outside that shared space records which insert is currently intended. Copying a kit’s inventory card is not the same as duplicating every borrowed tool, just as copying pointer members does not copy the objects they designate.
topics.principle:
A struct gives named members distinct storage within one aggregate. Use the dot operator for an object and arrow for a pointer; struct assignment copies member values, including embedded arrays, but pointer members remain aliases to the same pointees. Alignment is an implementation requirement, not universally equal to a type’s size.

Padding may occur between members and after the final member, so use sizeof and offsetof rather than guessed layouts. A union reserves storage sufficient for its largest member, suitably aligned; its size does not change when another member is stored. Pair a union with an enum tag to describe the intended active representation.

Compare structures member by member because padding makes raw memcmp unsuitable for general value equality. Portable persistence needs an explicit format rather than a memory dump.
topics.formula:
p->member ≡ (*p).member
Typical padded size = round_up(end_of_last_member, alignment)
Tagged value invariant: tag identifies the initialized union member
topics.symbols:
The arrow equivalence applies when p validly points to a live structure or union with the named member. The size expression is an explanatory layout model for typical implementations, not a universal C ABI formula; alignment and member offsets must be obtained from the implementation. The tagged-value statement is an invariant, not arithmetic.

An enum supplies named integer constants, while the program must keep its tag consistent with whichever union member was initialized and is intended to be read.
topics.example:
Assume char size and alignment are 1, int size and alignment are 4, and struct alignment is 4. For struct Packet { char kind; int count; char flag; }, kind occupies offset 0, padding occupies 1–3, count occupies 4–7 and flag occupies 8. Tail padding extends the size to 12. Reordering to int count; char kind; char flag; permits a typical size of 8 under these assumptions.

A union containing that int and a 20-byte character array needs at least 20 bytes, possibly more for alignment. Storing an int does not shrink it to four bytes.
topics.pitfall: Writing a raw struct to disk includes padding and machine-specific representations, and pointer values cannot reconstruct the pointed-to data in a later process.

check.question: If struct A contains int *data, what does b=a copy?
check.answer: It copies the pointer value, so both structures initially refer to the same allocation. Independent ownership needs a deliberate deep copy or an explicitly shared-ownership policy.

glossary.meaning: A named component stored within a structure or union.
Storage bytes inserted by an implementation to satisfy layout requirements.
Shared member storage paired with a tag that identifies the intended representation.

guided_questions.question: Does structure assignment clone pointed-to objects?
guided_questions.answer: No. Embedded arrays are copied, but pointer member values continue to designate the same objects.

guided_questions.question: Can memcmp generally test structure value equality?
guided_questions.answer: No. Padding and representation details can differ. Compare the logical members explicitly.

guided_questions.question: Who keeps a union tag consistent?
guided_questions.answer: The program. An enum label alone does not automatically control which union member was initialized.

instructor_notes.title: Persist meaning instead of addresses
instructor_notes.body: A file format should encode each logical field with a specified width and byte order. Process pointers and padding are unsuitable as portable saved data.

instructor_notes.title: Make representation changes local
instructor_notes.body: A tagged-value accessor can check the tag before reading. Centralizing that check reduces the chance that a new variant leaves old readers using the wrong member.

code_examples.title: Copy embedded data and share pointed-to data
code_examples.intro: Compare two kinds of structure member after one assignment.
code_examples.output:
original label=oak value=9
copy label=Oak value=9
code_examples.explanation:
Structure assignment copies the embedded label array into distinct storage. Changing the copy’s label therefore leaves the original label lowercase.

The borrowed pointer value is also copied, but the pointed-to integer array is not. Both structures observe the update to nine. The borrowed array remains alive throughout main, and neither structure owns a heap allocation here.
walkthrough: Create an embedded label and a pointer to shared data.
Copy the structure, then modify one member of each kind.
Compare which changes cross the copy boundary.

syntax_notes.meaning: Declare a type grouping named fields with distinct storage.
Copy the structure value, including the embedded array but only the pointer value.
Follow a pointer member to a shared object; structure copying did not create a new pointee.

code_examples.title: Read a union through its tag
code_examples.intro: Keep one tag and one initialized member in agreement.
code_examples.explanation:
The designated initializer names count as the initial union member. The COUNT tag records that choice. The accessor selects the matching member before interpreting the stored value.

Changing to temperature writes the new representation and changes the tag before the next call. This is a single-threaded update; concurrent readers would require synchronization around the whole change. Union storage does not shrink or grow between variants.
walkthrough: Initialize the count member together with its tag.
Select a member through a switch on the tag.
Change both representation and tag before reading again.

topics.title: File streams, binary records and errors
topics.story:
A notebook and an in-memory scratchpad both hold information, but their operations fail in different ways. Opening a notebook in a replacement mode may erase its old contents before any new page is written. A buffered pen can appear to have written while its ink is still waiting in the mechanism. C file streams similarly separate logical operations from the underlying device.

A short read may mean the notebook ended or that something went wrong; a final close can reveal a delayed write error. Careful file code treats every stage as an operation with a result, not merely a line of ceremony.
topics.principle:
fopen returns a stream pointer or NULL and interprets modes such as read, truncate-and-write and append. Standard streams are stdin, stdout and stderr. Formatted I/O converts text, while fread and fwrite transfer elements; their return values count complete elements, not bytes unless element size is one. fgetc returns int so every unsigned-char value can be distinguished from EOF.

Drive input loops using the read result, then distinguish end-of-file from error with feof and ferror. Seekable binary files can support fixed-record offsets; text-stream positioning has stricter portability constraints. Buffering means successful output may not yet have reached storage, so inspect fflush and fclose results when data matters.

Binary formats need specified field sizes, byte order and encoding to be portable across programs and machines.
topics.formula:
Byte count requested = element_size × element_count
Fixed-record offset = record_index × record_size
Read loop mnemonic: attempt → inspect result → process valid data → distinguish EOF/error
topics.symbols:
The element size and count are the second and third arguments of fread or fwrite. Their product is the requested byte count, but the return value reports how many complete elements were transferred. The record index is zero-based and the offset formula assumes a fixed-size binary format, a seekable stream and a representable offset.

The read-loop line is a control-flow mnemonic. EOF is a return indication; it is not a character stored at the end of every file.
topics.example:
A binary log format defines each record as exactly 12 bytes, independently of any C struct layout. To read zero-based record 4, seek to offset 4×12=48 and request one 12-byte element. A return value of 1 means the complete record arrived. A return value of 0 requires checking for an error or an incomplete final record before parsing.

If instead the program requests 12 elements of size one and receives 7, it knows seven bytes arrived but still lacks a full record. Opening the existing log with "wb" would truncate it; "rb" is appropriate for this read-only operation.
topics.pitfall: while (!feof(fp)) is not a correct input loop: the EOF indicator is usually set only after a read fails at the end, so stale data can be processed twice.

check.question: Why can a successful fprintf followed by a failing fclose matter?
check.answer: Buffered output can defer the actual write. A later flush during fclose can fail, so the earlier formatted-write result alone does not prove all data reached the file.

glossary.meaning: A C library object that manages buffered input or output.
A special input result distinct from all unsigned-char values.
One full element of the size requested from fread or fwrite.

guided_questions.question: Why keep fgetc in int?
guided_questions.answer: The result must represent every unsigned-char value plus the separate EOF indicator.

guided_questions.question: Does a short read always mean an error?
guided_questions.answer: No. It can mean end of input. Inspect ferror and whether the format required more data.

guided_questions.question: Why check close after successful writing?
guided_questions.answer: Buffered output may fail only when it is flushed during close.

guided_questions.question: Would fwrite(&record, sizeof record, 1, file) define the same portable format?
guided_questions.answer: No. Object layout, padding and byte order may differ. Explicitly encode the fields required by the file contract.

instructor_notes.title: Own temporary resources explicitly
instructor_notes.body: These examples create their own anonymous temporary streams with tmpfile and close them before exit. They require no prepared input files and do not overwrite user data.

instructor_notes.title: Choose transfer units consciously
instructor_notes.body: Reading bytes makes a truncated-record byte count visible. Reading larger elements reports only completed elements, so incomplete bytes must never be treated as a valid record.

code_examples.title: Read bytes until the operation reports the end
code_examples.intro: Include a zero byte to show that file input is not a C-string traversal.
code_examples.explanation:
The output stream receives three bytes, including a zero in the middle. Seeking switches from writing to reading and positions the stream at the start. fgetc returns zero for that byte, which is still ordinary data.

The loop stops only when the read returns EOF. The program then checks for an error and verifies the end indicator. All output operations that can fail on the temporary stream are checked; close is part of the result.
walkthrough: Write a known three-byte sequence to an owned temporary stream.
Seek and read using the return value as the loop condition.
Distinguish a zero byte, end of input and an input error.

syntax_notes.meaning: Create an owned temporary update stream. Check NULL before use; closing removes the temporary file.
Read one byte value or EOF using a result type that distinguishes them.
Inspect the error indicator after the read loop; EOF alone does not explain the cause.

code_examples.title: Count bytes and complete records separately
code_examples.intro: Read the same seven-byte input using two element sizes.
code_examples.output:
complete records=0
received bytes=7
truncated record rejected
code_examples.explanation:
A twelve-byte element cannot be completed from seven available bytes, so the first return count is zero. That count does not mean no underlying bytes were read. The program does not parse the incomplete record.

Seeking back resets the end-of-file indication. A second request uses one-byte elements, exposing the received count seven. The explicit format contract still requires twelve, so the record is rejected.
walkthrough: Request one complete twelve-byte record.
Rewind with a checked seek and request twelve one-byte elements.
Reject the input until all required record bytes exist.

code_examples.title: Define a file format instead of dumping a struct
code_examples.intro: Mina saves a sensor value on one computer and reads it on another. A raw struct dump makes the file depend on padding and byte order. She replaces that hidden agreement with four explicit bytes: a tag, a version, a high byte and a low byte. She can now write down exactly what a reader should accept before she writes the file code.
code_examples.output:
wire: 76 1 2 1
decoded: 513
bad version and short record rejected; output unchanged
walkthrough: Define each byte. The numeric tag 0x4c is 76; version 1 selects the only supported layout.
Split 513 into high=2 and low=1. Decode with value = 256*high + low.
Check write, seek, read-error and close results. Reading up to five bytes also exposes an unexpected extra byte in this one-record format.
Validate size, tag and version before assigning the caller output. Invalid input preserves the previous output value.
code_examples.explanation:
A struct describes an in-memory object, while a file format is an agreement between writers and readers. Here a record is exactly four eight-bit bytes, and the value is an unsigned integer from 0 to 65535. Endianness is explicit: the high byte comes first. Padding and host byte order never enter the file.

The bit operation value >> 8 removes the low eight bits. value & 255 keeps only those low bits. Decoding shifts the high byte back and combines the nonoverlapping parts with bitwise OR. For 513 = 2*256 + 1, the encoded pair is [2,1].

This is a minimal format, not a corruption detector. Many changed payloads remain valid records. A real format may need a checksum, length limits and a documented version migration. A checksum can detect some accidental corruption but does not authenticate a hostile sender. The source uses a temporary file so it cannot overwrite a learner file.

syntax_notes.meaning: An exact-width unsigned 16-bit integer on platforms that provide it.
Select the lowest eight bits.
Distinguish an I/O error from an ordinary short read at end of file.

topics.title: Dynamic allocation and object lifetime
topics.story:
A equipment desk lends numbered lockers on request. The locker number is useful only while the rental remains valid, and copying the number does not create a second locker. Returning the locker ends access for everyone holding a copy, even if the original renter crosses their own number out. Dynamic memory has the same ownership problem.

Resizing may move the contents to another locker, invalidating old directions. A disciplined program names who allocates, who may borrow, who may resize and who eventually frees each object. This bookkeeping is more important than memorizing the four allocation function names.
topics.principle:
malloc obtains uninitialized storage, calloc initializes allocated bytes to zero, realloc changes a prior allocation and free releases it. Check size arithmetic before allocation so multiplication cannot wrap. In C, allocation results need no cast when assigned to an object pointer, but the correct header is required.

Byte-zeroed storage is not a portable promise that every pointer representation is null or every floating representation is zero. For a nonzero realloc request, failure leaves the original allocation intact; use a temporary pointer and update ownership only on success. Successful reallocation invalidates old pointers into the allocation even when the address appears unchanged.

Free exactly the owned allocation base once, after all borrowers are finished. Automatic object lifetime ends when its enclosing execution scope ends; typical stack and heap diagrams are implementation models, not a universal layout guarantee.
topics.formula:
Allocation precondition: n ≤ SIZE_MAX / sizeof(*p)
Requested bytes = n × sizeof(*p)
Ownership invariant: one clear release responsibility per allocation
Lifetime: allocate → initialize → use → release
topics.symbols:
n is the desired element count and SIZE_MAX the largest size_t value. The division-based precondition prevents overflow before multiplication; sizeof(*p) uses the pointed-to type and does not dereference p for ordinary non-VLA types. Ownership and lifetime lines are design invariants, not numeric laws. The allocator may return NULL, so arithmetic validity is only the first check.

A pointer value can remain stored after release, but that does not preserve the lifetime of the old object.
topics.example:
Assume an int occupies four bytes. A six-element dynamic buffer requests 6×4=24 bytes. After initialization, growing to ten elements requests 40 bytes using a temporary realloc result. If it is NULL, the original six-element buffer still exists and must eventually be freed. If it succeeds, use the returned pointer and initialize elements 6–9 before reading them; new bytes are not automatically initialized.

A second pointer that previously referred to element 2 must be recomputed from the new base. Freeing the allocation and setting the owner to NULL does not repair any other stale aliases.
topics.pitfall: Returning the address of a local automatic variable leaves the caller with a pointer to an object whose lifetime has ended. Return a value or define a valid longer-lived ownership arrangement.

check.question: Why is p=realloc(p,new_size) risky when new_size is nonzero?
check.answer: On failure it overwrites the only saved allocation pointer with NULL, losing access to the still-allocated block. A temporary preserves the original owner until success is known.

glossary.meaning: The code responsible for releasing an allocation exactly once.
Code allowed to use an object while its lifetime and contract remain valid.
A pointer associated with an object whose lifetime has ended.

guided_questions.question: Does free repair every alias?
guided_questions.answer: No. Other stored pointers do not become safe merely because the owner was freed or set to NULL.

guided_questions.question: Why check multiplication before malloc?
guided_questions.answer: A wrapped size can request too little storage even if allocation succeeds.

guided_questions.question: What survives failed nonzero realloc?
guided_questions.answer: The original allocation remains valid. Preserve its pointer in a separate owner variable.

guided_questions.question: Why must length change after reserve succeeds?
guided_questions.answer: Length promises that those elements exist and are initialized. Increasing it before a failed allocation would make the metadata promise data that was never stored.

instructor_notes.title: Separate count from capacity
instructor_notes.body: An allocation can have space for ten values while only six are initialized. Reading newly added capacity before initialization is a separate error from being within allocated bounds.

instructor_notes.title: Resize invalidates borrowed locations
instructor_notes.body: After successful realloc, reconstruct interior pointers from the returned base and saved indices. Do not compare or reuse the old pointer as evidence that an alias survived.

code_examples.title: Start here: one allocation, one owner, one release
code_examples.intro: Follow a three-element allocation before adding resizing or linked structures.
code_examples.output:
values=10,20,30
owner cleared=yes
releasing a null owner is allowed
code_examples.explanation:
The program reserves room, checks success, initializes every element, uses the data and releases it. malloc returns uninitialized storage. The fixed count three makes the byte multiplication safe here; a general allocator must also check multiplication bounds.

release_values receives the address of the caller’s pointer. One star reads that pointer; another level would reach an int. The helper frees the allocation and then clears the caller’s owner. Calling free on NULL is allowed. Clearing one owner does not clear other aliases: this example deliberately creates none. The helper requires a valid address of a pointer that is NULL or owns an allocation accepted by free.
walkthrough: Count elements and use sizeof the pointed-to type.
Check allocation before initializing or reading the elements.
Release through the owner and observe the cleared pointer without accessing freed data.

syntax_notes.meaning: Measure one int without evaluating an uninitialized element.
Point to the caller’s int pointer so the helper can reset it.
Return this allocation; it is also valid when *owner is NULL.

code_examples.title: Allocate, initialize, use and release
code_examples.intro: Check size arithmetic and allocation as two separate conditions.
code_examples.explanation:
sizeof *values uses the pointed-to int type; for this ordinary non-VLA type it does not read through the initially null pointer. The division guard runs before multiplication.

After allocation succeeds, each element is written before it contributes to the sum. One owner releases the base pointer exactly once. Setting that owner to NULL helps avoid accidental reuse here, but it would not repair other aliases.
walkthrough: Validate the requested byte count without overflowing it.
Initialize every element before reading it.
Release the allocation and stop using its old addresses.

syntax_notes.meaning: Reject an element count whose byte-size multiplication would overflow size_t.
Allocate enough storage for n pointed-to elements; check the returned pointer before use.
End the owned allocation’s lifetime once all uses are finished.

code_examples.title: Commit a resize only after success
code_examples.intro: Keep the old allocation reachable if a nonzero resize fails.
code_examples.explanation:
The temporary resized receives the result. A failed nonzero request leaves values available for cleanup. Success replaces ownership with the returned pointer before any further access.

The first three initialized values are preserved. The newly available two elements are explicitly initialized. The program makes no assumption about whether the allocator moved storage and keeps no interior aliases across the resize.
walkthrough: Initialize the original allocation.
Use a temporary result and commit ownership after success.
Initialize new elements and release the returned allocation base.

code_examples.title: Grow an owned array without losing it
code_examples.intro: A sensor starts with two readings and keeps producing more. Mina allocates a larger array whenever space runs out. Her first sketch assigns realloc directly to the only pointer. If allocation fails, she can no longer find the old allocation. She rewrites the operation as a small transaction: check the requested size, ask for memory through a temporary pointer, and update the owner only after success.
code_examples.output:
length=1 capacity=2
length=2 capacity=2
length=3 capacity=4
length=4 capacity=4
length=5 capacity=8
oversized request rejected: 1
last value: 50
owner reset after free
walkthrough: Maintain length <= capacity. Only entries below length are initialized readings.
Check need against SIZE_MAX / sizeof(element) before multiplying. Check doubling before it can overflow.
Keep the old pointer until realloc succeeds. On failure, the old allocation and metadata still describe the same vector.
Append only after reserve succeeds. Free exactly once, then reset the owner so the empty state is explicit.
code_examples.explanation:
The vector owns its allocation. reserve borrows the owner temporarily; it does not create a second owner. The successful realloc may move storage, so pointers to elements must be treated as invalid after a successful resize. Store an index across growth, then obtain a fresh element pointer.

For five appends, capacities are 2, 2, 4, 4, 8. Under a model that copies all old elements on growth, the later growths copy 2 + 4 = 6 values. Doubling makes total copying over n appends O(n), so append has O(1) amortized cost. One particular append may still cost O(n). This is a cost model, not a claim that realloc always copies.

The rejected SIZE_MAX request tests arithmetic protection, not a real operating-system out-of-memory event. A larger test suite should inject allocation failure and verify unchanged contents. The example uses nonzero allocations and assumes a valid Vector created by this interface. It is not a concurrent container.

syntax_notes.meaning: Use the pointed-to element type when calculating bytes.
Hold a possible replacement without losing the original owner.
A compound literal that resets every member to zero.

topics.title: Linked lists and structural invariants
topics.story:
A treasure trail stores the next location on each clue card. Adding a card between two existing cards changes directions rather than shifting every later card. But finding the insertion place still requires following the trail unless someone already knows it. A doubly linked trail also keeps directions backward.

A circular trail returns to its start instead of ending, so an explorer who waits for an end marker walks forever. Linked-list programming succeeds when every update preserves a clear structural invariant and when a card is not destroyed before its next direction has been saved.
topics.principle:
A singly linked node holds payload and a next pointer. Maintain a head pointer, optionally a tail, and a documented empty representation. Inserting after a known node takes constant pointer updates; locating a position is generally linear. Deleting a node requires reconnecting its predecessor or updating the head, then releasing the removed node only after needed links are saved.

A pointer-to-pointer can uniformly represent the link that leads to a node, including the head link. Doubly linked lists maintain reciprocal next and previous links, enabling constant-time removal of a known node when ownership is clear. Circular lists use a start or sentinel-based stopping condition. Allocation failure must leave the old structure valid.

Persist payloads and reconstruct links later; raw process addresses are not a portable list format.
topics.formula:
Singly linked invariant: head reaches each live node once, then NULL
Doubly linked invariant: x->next->prev = x when x->next exists
Search: O(n); splice at a known valid link: O(1)
Reverse step: save next; redirect current->next; advance
topics.symbols:
n counts nodes and the complexity assumes ordinary pointer access. A splice changes a fixed number of links once the location is known; it does not include a search. The displayed equalities and sequence are invariants and a mnemonic rather than quantitative laws. The doubly linked condition requires valid non-null nodes and has a corresponding previous-to-next condition.

Circular structures replace the NULL-terminated invariant with a specified cycle or sentinel invariant and must use matching traversal and destruction rules.
topics.example:
Start with a singly linked list 4→7→9→NULL. To remove 7, keep a pointer to node 4 and a temporary pointer to node 7. Save node 7’s next pointer, set node 4’s next to node 9, and then free node 7. The result is 4→9→NULL. To reverse it, start previous=NULL and current=4. Save 9, redirect 4.next to NULL, then advance.

Save NULL, redirect 9.next to 4, then advance again. Set head to previous, giving 9→4→NULL. Each next pointer is saved before mutation so the unprocessed suffix remains reachable.
topics.pitfall: A constant-time deletion claim assumes the needed link or predecessor is already known. Finding a node by value in a singly linked list remains O(n).

check.question: Why must deleting the head update the caller’s head variable?
check.answer: The old first node is no longer part of the list. Return the new head or pass a pointer to the head pointer; changing only a local copy leaves the caller pointing to the removed node.

glossary.meaning: The pointer variable that identifies the first node or NULL.
Changing a fixed number of links to insert or remove nodes at a known position.
A pointer used to reach and update another pointer variable.

guided_questions.question: Why save next before free?
guided_questions.answer: After release, reading even the removed node’s link is invalid. Save every needed value first.

guided_questions.question: Is deletion by value constant time?
guided_questions.answer: Generally no. The search is linear even when the final link update is constant time.

guided_questions.question: What must allocation failure preserve?
guided_questions.answer: All existing reachable nodes and links must remain valid, with ownership still clear.

instructor_notes.title: Separate search from mutation
instructor_notes.body: First identify the link that must change. Then perform a small update with a clear before-and-after invariant. Pointer-to-pointer code makes the head case part of the same operation.

instructor_notes.title: Changing termination changes every traversal
instructor_notes.body: A circular list cannot reuse a NULL-terminated destruction loop unchanged. Choose the structural invariant before implementing iteration, reversal and cleanup.

code_examples.title: Remove both a middle node and the head
code_examples.intro: Represent the incoming link explicitly so both cases use one function.
code_examples.explanation:
The link variable points either to head or to a predecessor’s next field. This unifies the two places where an incoming edge can live. The search stops at the matching node or a NULL link.

On a match, the incoming link is redirected before the victim is freed. Allocation checks preserve the already built list, and the failure path destroys it. Final cleanup saves next before releasing each node.
walkthrough: Build a checked, owned NULL-terminated list.
Search for the incoming link and reconnect it.
Free only removed nodes, then destroy the remaining list.

syntax_notes.meaning: Point to the variable that currently leads to a node, including the head variable itself.
Reconnect the incoming link before releasing the removed node.
Move to the address of the next link while searching.

code_examples.title: Reverse links without losing the suffix
code_examples.intro: Use automatic nodes to focus on link order without allocation.
code_examples.explanation:
previous owns no allocation; it identifies the already reversed prefix. head identifies the unprocessed suffix. Saving next keeps that suffix reachable before the current edge is redirected.

All three nodes are automatic objects alive until main returns. They must not be passed to free. Reversal changes links, not payload values or storage ownership.
walkthrough: Maintain separate pointers for reversed and unprocessed portions.
Save the next link before redirecting it.
Adopt the reversed prefix as the new head after the suffix is empty.

topics.title: Function pointers and behavioral parameters
topics.story: A theatre has many light controls. Each control accepts a small action card. The same control can dim a lamp, change its colour, or switch it off. The control does not need to know every action in advance.
topics.principle:
A function pointer can be stored, passed and called, enabling callbacks and dispatch tables. Parentheses distinguish a pointer to a function from a function returning a pointer. The function’s return and parameter types must be compatible with the pointer type used to call it; casting away a mismatch does not make the call valid. typedef can make callback declarations easier to read.

A qsort comparator receives pointers to elements and returns a negative, zero or positive result according to a consistent ordering. Compare integer values with relational operators rather than subtraction that can overflow. Validate a table index and non-null function pointer before dispatch. ISO C does not generally equate object pointers and function pointers; dynamic loading uses platform-specific guarantees beyond portable ISO C.
topics.formula:
int (*op)(int,int): pointer to function taking two ints and returning int
int *op(int,int): function returning pointer to int
Safe integer comparator result: (a > b) − (a < b)
topics.symbols:
The parentheses bind *op before the function parameter list, making op a pointer to a function. Without them, op names a function whose result is an int pointer. In the comparator expression, a and b are integer values, and each relational expression produces zero or one. Subtracting those small results safely returns −1, 0 or 1.

This defines ascending numeric order without evaluating a−b, whose mathematical difference may not fit in int.
topics.example:
A calculator defines two compatible functions, sum(int,int) and difference(int,int), and a table of function pointers containing them. With operands 17 and 6, dispatch index 0 calls sum and returns 23; index 1 calls difference and returns 11. Index 2 must be rejected before indexing because the table has two entries.

For sorting integers −2000000000 and 2000000000 on a 32-bit-int implementation, direct subtraction cannot represent the difference. The relational comparator instead evaluates 0−1=−1 for the first ordering, correctly reporting that the negative value comes first without overflow or assumptions about wrapping.
topics.pitfall: Passing a function with the wrong signature and casting its address to the expected callback type can produce undefined behavior when called.

check.question: Why should a comparator return zero for values it considers equivalent?
check.answer: The sorting algorithm relies on a consistent ordering relation. Contradictory answers can invalidate its assumptions and make the result meaningless.

glossary.meaning: A function passed as behavior for another operation to invoke.
A typed pointer used to designate and call a compatible function.
A callback reporting negative, zero or positive according to an ordering.

guided_questions.question: Can a cast fix an incompatible callback signature?
guided_questions.answer: No. Calling through an incompatible function type can be undefined behavior.

guided_questions.question: Why avoid a-b in an integer comparator?
guided_questions.answer: The mathematical difference may overflow even when both inputs individually fit.

guided_questions.question: Why check a dispatch index first?
guided_questions.answer: Accessing the table out of bounds is already invalid before any function call occurs.

instructor_notes.title: Behavior is also part of an API
instructor_notes.body: A callback contract includes argument lifetime, permitted side effects and ordering consistency, not only its C type. A type-compatible callback can still violate the algorithm’s assumptions.

instructor_notes.title: Keep error policy outside arithmetic
instructor_notes.body: A dispatch table selects behavior but does not validate arithmetic ranges automatically. Small fixed operands are safe here; external operands need operation-specific overflow checks.

code_examples.title: Start here: pass one operation into a loop
code_examples.intro: Separate visiting each element from deciding what to do with it.
code_examples.explanation:
The loop is a mail carrier visiting three addresses. The callback is the instruction about what to do at each address. The loop calls the supplied function with one integer and prints its result. The original array stays unchanged.

Transform names a pointer to a function taking int and returning int. Parentheses around *Transform distinguish a pointer to function from other declarations. Both callbacks match that type. The caller supplies a non-null compatible function and a valid array range. The arithmetic is safe for the fixed small inputs; these callbacks are not overflow-safe transformations for every int.
walkthrough: Define the exact function signature required by the loop.
Run the same visiting logic with two different behaviors.
Print the unchanged input to distinguish transformation from mutation.

syntax_notes.meaning: Give this compatible function-pointer type a readable name.
Call the supplied function with the current element.
This function reads through this pointer without writing the input.

code_examples.title: Select behavior through a checked table
code_examples.intro: Use one compatible function-pointer type and reject an invalid index.
code_examples.explanation:
Both functions match the typedef exactly. The table stores their addresses, and calling through an entry supplies the same two argument types.

The loop deliberately reaches the first invalid index. The guard rejects it before table access. This separates operation selection from the arithmetic performed by the selected callback.
walkthrough: Declare one shared callback type.
Validate the index before reading a table entry.
Invoke the selected behavior with bounded operands.

syntax_notes.meaning: Give a readable name to a pointer to a two-int function returning int.
Declare an array of compatible function pointers.
Call the selected function after validating the index.

code_examples.title: Sort without subtracting arbitrary integers
code_examples.intro: Compare extreme values safely, then sort a small array with duplicates.
code_examples.explanation:
qsort passes addresses of actual int elements through its generic pointer interface. The comparator converts back to the correct element pointer type before reading.

Each relational expression is zero or one, so their difference lies between minus one and one. It never evaluates the potentially overflowing difference between the integer values themselves. Equal duplicate values return zero. qsort does not promise stable ordering of equal elements.
walkthrough: Recover the actual element types from the generic pointers.
Use relational results instead of subtracting the original values.
Sort and inspect the complete result including duplicates.

topics.title: Preprocessing, macros and conditional builds
topics.story:
A printing press prepares a document by inserting standard paragraphs and replacing abbreviations before the editor checks the resulting sentences. The C preprocessor plays a similar role before type checking. It does not understand that a repeated abbreviation may perform a side effect twice. Conditional sections decide which source text reaches the compiler, while header guards stop the same declarations from being inserted repeatedly in one translation unit.

Thinking in terms of the expanded document helps diagnose surprises: inspect what the compiler actually receives, rather than assuming a macro behaves like a normal function call with evaluated arguments.
topics.principle:
Preprocessing handles includes, macro replacement, conditional compilation and source-location control. Object-like macros replace names; function-like macros substitute argument tokens. Parenthesize each argument and the complete result where appropriate, but parentheses do not prevent multiple evaluation or unsequenced side effects.

Prefer a static inline function for typed computation that should evaluate each argument once. Include guards avoid duplicate inclusion within one translation unit; they do not solve multiple external definitions across translation units. #ifdef tests whether a macro exists, while #if can test its numeric value. __FILE__ and __LINE__ help diagnostics; __func__ is a predefined function-scope identifier rather than a preprocessing macro. #line changes diagnostic source locations.

Pragmas are implementation-specific unless standardized, so distinguish portable source from compiler extensions.
topics.formula:
SQUARE(x) defined as ((x)*(x))
SQUARE(a+1) expands to ((a+1)*(a+1))
SQUARE(i++) expands to ((i++)*(i++)) — undefined behavior in C
Mnemonic: preprocess → inspect expansion → type-check
topics.symbols:
SQUARE is a macro name and x a token parameter, not a runtime local variable. Parentheses preserve grouping for an argument such as a+1. Repeating i++ duplicates a modification, and the multiplication does not sequence the two modifications of i, causing undefined behavior. The final line is a workflow mnemonic, not an equation.

An inline function evaluates the caller’s argument once, although a caller can still create unsequenced interactions between multiple function arguments in C.
topics.example:
With a=4, the unparenthesized macro #define BAD(x) x*x expands BAD(a+1) to a+1*a+1, which evaluates as 4+4+1=9. The parenthesized version gives (4+1)×(4+1)=25. For #define ENABLE_CACHE 0, #ifdef ENABLE_CACHE includes its branch because the name is defined, whereas #if ENABLE_CACHE excludes its branch because its numeric value is zero.

A static inline int square(int x) returning x*x safely computes square(i++) once for an initial i=4: it returns 16 and leaves i=5, assuming the multiplication is representable and no other conflicting expression accesses i.
topics.pitfall: Header guards are scoped to each preprocessing run. Defining an externally linked global object in a guarded header can still create one definition in every .c file that includes it.

check.question: Why can parentheses fix BAD(a+1) but not SQUARE(i++)?
check.answer: Parentheses repair expression grouping. They do not turn duplicated tokens into one evaluated value or sequence the two increments.

glossary.meaning: Replacement of preprocessing tokens before ordinary C type checking.
The source remaining after a source file and its included text are preprocessed.
Evaluating an argument expression more than once because its tokens were duplicated.

guided_questions.question: Do parentheses prevent duplicate evaluation?
guided_questions.answer: No. They control grouping, not how many copies of an argument are evaluated.

guided_questions.question: Is a macro with value zero undefined?
guided_questions.answer: No. #ifdef sees a defined name; #if evaluates its numeric condition.

guided_questions.question: Why use static inline for small arithmetic?
guided_questions.answer: It supplies type checking and evaluates each argument once inside the call; it is still subject to normal arithmetic limits.

instructor_notes.title: Inspect the expanded program
instructor_notes.body: Compiler preprocessing output exposes token substitution. Use it to explain a macro failure before changing unrelated compiler options.

instructor_notes.title: Choose configuration semantics explicitly
instructor_notes.body: A numeric feature macro can represent disabled with zero. A presence-only macro uses defined versus absent. Mixing these conventions silently changes builds.

code_examples.title: Compare token substitution with a function call
code_examples.intro: Demonstrate a grouping bug without ever executing an unsafe repeated increment.
code_examples.explanation:
BAD(a+1) expands into a+1*a+1, so multiplication binds before the additions and gives nine. SQUARE groups both copies and gives twenty-five.

The increment is passed only to the real function, which receives the old value four once and leaves i at five. Calling SQUARE(i++) would cause unsequenced modifications and is deliberately absent. Parentheses alone would not make it safe.
walkthrough: Expand the faulty macro mentally before evaluating it.
Compare the parenthesized arithmetic result.
Use a real function for the side-effecting argument.

syntax_notes.meaning: Replace argument tokens twice without grouping; this is intentionally a faulty arithmetic macro.
Protect grouping but still duplicate the argument tokens. Do not pass side effects.
Declare a typed function with translation-unit-local linkage; its parameter is one evaluated value.

code_examples.title: Distinguish presence from numeric truth
code_examples.intro: A defined zero feature flag answers two different questions.
code_examples.output:
macro exists
cache disabled
active function=main
code_examples.explanation:
The preprocessor includes the first branch because the name exists, but includes the second else branch because its numeric value is zero. The compiler only receives the selected statements.

__func__ supplies the enclosing function’s name as a predefined function-scope identifier. It is not a user macro and does not require a guessed file path or line number in the expected output.
walkthrough: Define the feature flag explicitly as zero.
Compare the source selected by #ifdef and #if.
Inspect the predefined function name in ordinary runtime output.

topics.title: Translation units, symbols and libraries
topics.story:
A theater production has scripts prepared independently by several writers. Each script can mention a performer supplied elsewhere, but before opening night the producer must match every reference with an appropriate performer. Compilation checks an individual translation unit; linking connects its external references to definitions.

A private helper resembles a performer known only inside one rehearsal room. A shared library supplies performers loaded through a runtime system, while a static archive contributes selected object code to the executable. Naming a performer in the program booklet does not hire them, just as including a header does not necessarily link the corresponding implementation.
topics.principle:
A typical C toolchain preprocesses source, compiles it to assembly, assembles object files and links them into a program. Headers provide declarations and shared types; a non-inline external function normally has one definition supplied by some translation unit or library. An extern declaration can refer to a global defined elsewhere; file-scope static gives internal linkage.

Scope, linkage and storage duration are separate concepts. Object files contain code, data, relocation information and symbol tables in a platform-specific format. Static libraries are archives from which required members may be selected; command-line order can matter. Shared-library linking records runtime dependencies, and explicit dynamic loading uses facilities such as dlopen and dlsym on supporting platforms.

Diagnose missing definitions, duplicate definitions and incompatible declarations before guessing at compiler flags.
topics.symbols:
The arrows summarize a conventional toolchain rather than specifying the internal design of every compiler. A declaration tells a translation unit the name and type of add; a definition also provides its body. The addition example assumes representable operands. GCC-style -E, -S and -c stop the driver at different stages.

An object file can contain unresolved external references that are acceptable until linking; a header include is source inclusion, not a command to load library code.
topics.example:
Suppose main.c includes math_ops.h, whose only content is the declaration int add(int,int), and calls add(8,5). Compiling main.c to main.o succeeds because the compiler knows the interface, but linking main.o alone cannot supply add’s implementation. Compile math_ops.c, which defines add, and link both objects; the program can then compute 13.

If two .c files both define int total=0 with external linkage, including guards does not fix the duplicate definition. Place one definition in one .c file and an extern int total declaration in the shared header. Inspect object symbols when the source organization and linker message disagree.
topics.pitfall: Compilation success does not prove declarations across separately compiled files are compatible. Keep shared interfaces in headers and include them in their implementation files too.

check.question: What does static on a file-scope helper function accomplish?
check.answer: It gives the name internal linkage, keeping that function’s identity within its translation unit. Another translation unit can use the same helper name for its own distinct function.

glossary.meaning: A statement introducing an identifier and its type to the compiler.
A declaration that also supplies an object or function implementation.
The rule determining whether declarations denote the same entity across scopes or translation units.

guided_questions.question: Does including a header supply every function body?
guided_questions.answer: No. Headers normally provide interfaces; implementations must still be linked when required.

guided_questions.question: Are scope and lifetime the same?
guided_questions.answer: No. A local static object has block scope but retains its value throughout program execution.

guided_questions.question: What does file-scope static hide?
guided_questions.answer: It gives the identifier internal linkage, distinct from same-named entities in other translation units.

instructor_notes.title: Share one interface declaration
instructor_notes.body: In a multi-file project, include the same header in both callers and the implementation. This lets the compiler compare the implementation with its advertised type.

instructor_notes.title: A standalone example has a deliberate limit
instructor_notes.body: The first program places a declaration and definition in one file to remain directly runnable. Real separate-compilation diagnosis additionally requires compiling and linking distinct translation units.

code_examples.title: Use an interface before its definition
code_examples.intro: Keep declaration, definition and a private helper distinct in one runnable translation unit.
code_examples.explanation:
The prototype states the argument and return types. The later function definition supplies executable behavior. The extern declaration refers to the single total definition rather than creating a second initialized object.

helper has internal linkage and supports add without becoming part of its public interface. All definitions are present in this standalone file; the example does not pretend to reproduce a missing-object linker failure.
walkthrough: Read the prototypes as promises about types.
Locate the unique definitions satisfying those promises.
Call the public function and observe the linked object value.

syntax_notes.meaning: Declare a function interface before its body is seen. The semicolon ends the declaration.
Declare an externally linked object defined once elsewhere in the program. Here that definition is later in the same file.
Give a helper internal linkage, preventing this name from becoming a shared external definition.

code_examples.title: Separate local scope from storage duration
code_examples.intro: Compare an automatic local with a static local over repeated calls.
code_examples.output:
automatic=1 persistent=1
automatic=1 persistent=2
automatic=1 persistent=3
code_examples.explanation:
Both local names are visible only within inspect. The automatic object is initialized to zero for each call, while the static local is initialized once and retains its value.

The static before inspect itself has a different role: it gives the function internal linkage. One keyword participates in different rules depending on declaration context. These calls are single-threaded; unsynchronized concurrent increments would require a different design.
walkthrough: Observe that both variables have the same lexical scope.
Track which initialization occurs on every call.
Distinguish object storage duration from function linkage.

topics.title: Signals and asynchronous safety
topics.story:
A stage manager can ring a bell at almost any moment to request that a performance stop. The performer should record the request and finish a safe transition, rather than trying to rebuild the stage while an interrupted worker holds tools in an unknown state. A signal handler has the same interruption problem: it may run while library code is halfway through modifying its internal data.

Setting a small flag is often enough; ordinary control flow can then perform cleanup. A bell also does not count every audience member who rang it, just as standard signals may coalesce rather than queue every event.
topics.principle:
Signals notify a process or thread of asynchronous events such as interruption, termination requests or child status changes. On POSIX systems, sigaction gives controlled handler installation and masking. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught or ignored. A handler must obey async-signal-safety rules; ordinary printf, malloc and mutex locking are inappropriate because interruption can encounter inconsistent state or deadlock.

A simple handler may assign a volatile sig_atomic_t flag and let normal code act on it; this special pattern does not make volatile a general thread-synchronization tool. Signal masks control delivery, and a robust wait protocol uses atomic mask-and-wait operations such as sigsuspend to avoid lost wakeups. Interrupted system calls may report EINTR or be restarted depending on the operation and configuration.

Symbolic signal names are portable across POSIX systems; numeric assignments vary.
topics.formula:
Mnemonic: handler records request → main flow checks flag → cleanup runs normally
Race-prone sequence: check flag; pause()
Safer wait pattern: block signal; inspect predicate; sigsuspend with temporary mask
topics.symbols:
The arrows describe a control protocol, not elapsed-time guarantees. A flag is an object of volatile sig_atomic_t used only in a manner permitted for a signal handler; an idempotent stop request is simpler than a count of events. The predicate is the state that tells ordinary code whether work is ready or shutdown is requested.

The mask determines which signals are blocked. Atomically changing the mask while waiting closes the gap in which a signal could arrive after a check but before sleeping.
topics.example:
A worker sets stop_requested=0 and installs a SIGTERM handler that only assigns stop_requested=1. After each completed work item, normal code checks the flag. If a termination request arrives during item 7, the handler returns quickly; the worker completes item 7, observes the flag, closes its stream and releases its allocation in ordinary control flow.

A loop that instead checks the flag and then calls pause can sleep forever if the signal arrives between those actions and no later signal occurs. The block-check-sigsuspend pattern addresses that ordering gap. Multiple SIGTERM arrivals need not be counted because shutdown is an idempotent request.
topics.pitfall: Calling a function from normal threaded code safely does not mean it is async-signal-safe. Thread safety and signal-handler safety are different contracts.

check.question: Why is a sleep call not a reliable substitute for waiting on a signal condition?
check.answer: Sleep merely delays execution. It does not atomically coordinate the predicate check with signal delivery, and timing changes can expose the same missed-notification race.

glossary.meaning: A function entered when a caught signal is delivered.
The set of signals whose delivery is currently blocked.
Permitted by the signal contract even if an interrupted operation was in progress.

guided_questions.question: Why avoid printf in a handler?
guided_questions.answer: It may interrupt library state that is not safe to reenter. Record a permitted flag and print in ordinary flow.

guided_questions.question: Does volatile synchronize threads?
guided_questions.answer: No. The signal flag pattern has specific rules; volatile is not a substitute for thread synchronization.

guided_questions.question: Can a standard signal count every event?
guided_questions.answer: Not reliably. Repeated pending standard signals may coalesce; use an appropriate queued protocol for counts.

instructor_notes.title: Synchronous acceptance can simplify design
instructor_notes.body: A dedicated signal-waiting flow can block selected signals and accept them with sigwait, avoiding an asynchronous handler for those signals. Threaded programs must arrange masks before worker creation.

instructor_notes.title: Waiting is a protocol, not a delay
instructor_notes.body: A sleep does not close the gap between checking a flag and beginning to wait. Use a mask-and-wait design or synchronous signal acceptance with explicit ownership of the signal.

code_examples.title: Record a signal and handle it in normal flow
code_examples.intro: Raise one signal deterministically and keep output outside the handler.
code_examples.output:
request observed=yes
cleanup in normal flow
code_examples.explanation:
